messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert, a 62-year-old North American potter, had built most of his adult life around a quiet rhythm: the wheel turning, the clay centering under his hands, the kiln warming the studio behind his house where he lived with his wife. That rhythm was shattered when his brother died suddenly and unexpectedly. Robert had answered the phone expecting an ordinary conversation, only to hear that his brother was gone. There had been no warning, no chance to say goodbye, no gradual fading that might have prepared him for it. In the first days afterward, he moved through the practical demands of the funeral and the arrangements almost on autopilot, but the finality of the death stayed with him in a raw, almost physical way. He found himself staring at ordinary objects that had belonged to his brother and feeling as though they had become unbearable to touch, as if they carried the whole weight of what had happened.

In the months that followed, Robert became increasingly careful about what he let himself encounter. Anything that reminded him of his brother — old photographs, a particular song that had once played during family gatherings, even small personal items he had inherited or kept from him — became something he worked hard to avoid. He did not describe it as wanting to “move on”; rather, he felt that if he let himself look too closely at reminders, the loss would come rushing back all at once and leave him overwhelmed. So he began putting away mementos, leaving drawers unopened, and quietly changing the subject when family members brought up shared memories. At home, he would steer clear of rooms or objects that seemed to carry his brother’s presence. In his studio, where he spent long hours alone shaping bowls and mugs, he sometimes caught sight of pieces he had once intended to give as gifts or display at a show and felt a sudden tightening in his chest when they seemed to resemble something his brother would have admired. He would set those pieces aside, telling himself it was simpler not to think about them.

Over time, Robert also found himself turning away from positive feelings when they surfaced. Moments that might once have felt comforting — a good meal shared with his wife, a successful firing in the kiln, a day when the light fell beautifully across the shelves of finished work — now felt risky to him. He had come to believe that letting himself feel good made him vulnerable to a harder fall afterward, as if any warmth or pleasure invited the memory of how quickly life could change. When his wife tried to brighten a weekend with talk of a trip or a celebration, he often grew quiet or changed the subject. He did not want to be ungrateful, but he felt safest keeping his emotions flat, even when something went well. The same guardedness extended to the future. He stopped making plans far ahead, avoiding commitments that would require him to imagine months or years ahead, because future plans brought with them the unbearable assumption that life would keep unfolding as expected. Since his brother had died without warning, Robert felt he could not trust that anything he anticipated would still be there when the time came.

At home, these patterns gradually altered the texture of his marriage. His wife noticed that he no longer spoke easily about birthdays, holidays, or travel, and that he seemed to hold back whenever conversation turned hopeful or affectionate. In the studio, his avoidance left him more isolated, less willing to participate in shows or to accept invitations that would require planning ahead. He kept working, but more narrowly, sticking to the immediate task in front of him and resisting anything that asked him to look too far forward. Though he remained devoted to his craft, he found little comfort in imagining what might come next. Even small future-oriented questions — whether he might take on a new class, prepare for a market, or plan a visit — could make him feel cornered by uncertainty. Rather than risk that feeling, he would delay, postpone, or say no.

By the time Robert came for help, his score on the PCL-5 reflected the toll of these months of constriction. What finally brought him in was not a single dramatic moment but the growing sense that his world had become smaller and harder to inhabit. He was tired of living as though reminders were lurking everywhere, tired of bracing against any good feeling, and tired of refusing to think beyond the next day. What he feared most was that if he allowed himself to remember his brother fully, or to hope again, he would be swept under by the loss all over again. What he hoped for, though he found it hard to say aloud, was some way to carry the grief without having to keep sealing off so much of his life from it.
